schema_note: Mirrors INESCTEC_RESEARCH.pdf section 3/4 output schema exactly. hierarchical labels: subcase|supercase|same_level. pragmatic labels: revises|contradicts|resolves|depends_on|references. state_node types: goal|decision|constraint|open_question. retrieval_count is set equal to recurrence_count throughout, per the worked example's own convention for a static, hand-built corpus (real runs diverge). Entity taxonomy extended for this domain (per report section 3.2's note that the type list is domain-specific, not fixed): person, organization, system, tool, measurement, location, event, document, resource, endpoint. 'resource' = a named domain-model/API resource concept (e.g. Article, Topic). 'endpoint' = a concrete route/path once one is actually specified (e.g. /articles/{id}/topics/{topic_id}).

schema_findings.issue: Domain-model/resource nouns (e.g. 'Article', 'Topic', 'Entity' as API resource types) did not fit any original entity type (person, organization, system, tool, measurement, location, event, document).
schema_findings.proposed_direction: Resolved at N_6/N_7: added 'resource' and 'endpoint' as two new domain-specific entity types, per report section 3.2's explicit allowance that the type list is domain-specific. Retrofitted across N_1-N_6 below.

schema_findings.issue: N_1's answer uses 'Order' and 'OrderItems' as a generic illustrative example (ownership-boundary analogy), not as real resources of the application being designed.
schema_findings.proposed_direction: Deliberately left untagged as entities — tagging them as 'resource' type would misrepresent them as part of this application's actual domain model. Noted here so a future annotator doesn't 'fix' this as a missed extraction.

schema_findings.issue: state_node_links.relates can only target pre-existing open state nodes (per report W4 spec), not nodes created in the same turn — so a same-turn decision cannot formally be marked constrained_by a constraint created alongside it, even when the constraint clearly motivates the decision.
schema_findings.proposed_direction: Either (a) accept this as a real limitation and document it - motivating constraints should be stated in a prior turn if the link needs to be explicit, or (b) extend W4 to allow same-turn cross-references between its own creates. Not resolved here; Phase 3.2 decision.

schema_findings.issue: Corpus-construction QA gap: citations field values were repeatedly recorded without inserting the corresponding [N_x] bracket marker into the actual answer text (affected N_16, N_17, N_19, N_20, N_22, N_23), caught by the researcher rather than by process.
schema_findings.proposed_direction: Not a schema ambiguity - a corpus QA practice fix. Resolved by adding an automated post-commit check (citations field vs regex-extracted [N_x] brackets in answer text) run on every commit from this point forward, same pattern as the recurrence_count recomputation fix.

schema_findings.issue: Graph-model limitation: a newly created state node (e.g. SN_32, a cross-cutting design-principle constraint) cannot be retroactively linked back to earlier, already-committed decisions it conceptually generalizes over (N_12, N_14, N_18, N_24, N_26) - state_node_links can only be written at the turn where a node is created or subsequently referenced going forward, never backfilled onto past turns.
schema_findings.proposed_direction: Accept as an inherent property of an append-only interaction log (past turns are immutable), or consider a separate mechanism for retroactive pattern-tagging during Phase 3.2 / periodic consolidation passes if this kind of emergent cross-cutting principle turns out to be common and valuable enough to warrant it.

schema_findings.issue: No deprecation/supersession mechanism exists for entities: E_23 (/conversations) and E_24 (/conversations/{id}/messages) are now effectively superseded by E_35/E_36 (/me/-prefixed), but nothing in the schema marks that relationship - old and new endpoint entities simply coexist.
schema_findings.proposed_direction: Consider an optional superseded_by field on entity records, populated when a later decision revises an earlier-introduced endpoint/resource name. Not resolved here; Phase 3.2 decision.

schema_findings.issue: Edge case in the default epistemic_status rule (report 3.5): both turns are clarification_request, so they default to 'open', yet each turn's own answer fully resolves the question asked. No later turn sends a resolves edge, so they remain 'open' permanently despite being answered.
schema_findings.proposed_direction: The report itself flags this default as 'an engineering default, not an established fact' and asks Phase 3 to stress-test it. Two options: (a) allow a turn's own answer to close its epistemic status when it is self-contained, or (b) keep the mechanical rule and accept that 'open' means 'the speech act was a question type', not 'still unanswered'. Left as-is here so the edge case is preserved in the corpus rather than smoothed away.

schema_findings.issue: The epistemic-status state machine (report 3.5 edge->status table) was not applied during initial annotation: all 50 nodes were left at their creation default, so incoming revises/resolves/contradicts edges produced no status change and no epistemic_history entries. Caught only by a post-hoc audit against the spec.
schema_findings.proposed_direction: Fixed: statuses recomputed by replaying all epistemic edges in turn order, including no-op transitions which the spec says must still be logged for provenance. Recommend this replay be an automated invariant check in the pipeline's test suite, not a manual annotation step.

N_1.question: I want to start designing the REST API for this application. I already have a general idea of the data and features, but I don't want to jump straight into implementing endpoints. How would you approach the API architecture first? I'm particularly interested in how we should identify the main resources and organize the API before we start writing code.
N_1.answer: Model your domain first, independent of HTTP — list the core entities and how they relate, and decide ownership boundaries (e.g. does Order own OrderItems, or are items independently addressable?). That decision is what determines your URL structure later, not the other way around. Do you already have your main resources in mind, or want to work through that together first?
N_1.summary: Sets the goal of designing the API's resource model and organization before implementing endpoints.

N_2.question: I have some of them in mind from the application design. The main ones I currently see are User, Article, Source, Topic, and Entity. There will also be things around the RAG/chat side later. I'm not completely sure which of these should be treated as independent resources, though. Maybe we can go through them one by one and decide what should actually be exposed through the API.
N_2.answer: Sure — let's go one at a time. A good gut-check for each: is this something a client ever fetches, filters, or links to on its own, or does it only ever appear nested inside something else? If it's the former, it's a resource. If the latter, it's probably just a field or sub-object. Which one do you want to start with?
N_2.summary: Lists candidate resources (User, Article, Source, Topic, Entity) and proposes an addressability test to review them one by one.

N_3.question: Let's start with Article. It seems like the most central resource in the application, and I expect clients will need to fetch, search, filter, and probably relate articles to things like topics, sources, and entities. How would you model Article as a resource, and what would you consider its main relationships?
N_3.answer: Yes, Article should be top-level — it's clearly independently addressable per the test from before [N_2]. For relationships: Source is many-to-one (an Article has exactly one Source, via source_id); Topic and Entity are many-to-many, but I'd treat them differently — Topics are probably curated/editable so a normal join relationship works, while Entities are likely derived from NLP extraction, so I'd expose those as a read-only sub-resource (/articles/{id}/entities) rather than a client-editable link. Filtering becomes query params on the collection (/articles?topic_id=...&source_id=...).
N_3.summary: Decides Article is a top-level resource: Source many-to-one, Topic/Entity many-to-many, Entity exposed as a read-only sub-resource.

N_4.question: That makes sense. I especially like keeping the extracted Entity relationship read-only rather than letting clients modify something generated by the NLP pipeline. One thing I'm wondering about: if Topic is curated and many-to-many with Article, should clients be able to manage that relationship directly from the article side, like adding/removing topics from an article? Or would you keep topic assignment behind a separate service/API operation?
N_4.answer: I'd keep it as a dedicated relationship endpoint rather than letting clients edit a nested array directly — something like POST/DELETE /articles/{id}/topics/{topic_id}. That way you can validate against the curated topic list, dedupe, and log assignment changes in one place, instead of scattering that logic across a generic article PATCH. It's still 'from the article side' in terms of routing [N_3], just not folded into the article resource's own body.
N_4.summary: Decides Topic assignment on Article is managed via a dedicated relationship endpoint, not a nested field on the article resource.

N_5.question: For the Source relationship, since an article has exactly one source, would you just keep source_id as part of the article representation, or is there any reason to expose something like /articles/{id}/source as well?
N_5.answer: Keep source_id inline on the article representation — it's a single foreign key, not a collection, so there's no add/remove semantics the way Topic had. A dedicated sub-resource route only earns its place when something needs independent operations, and a 1:1 pointer doesn't. That said, this touches something we haven't actually settled yet [N_3]: whether Source itself should be independently listable as a top-level resource (/sources/{id}, /sources?...) — that's really still part of the open question from earlier [N_2], not resolved just by deciding how it's referenced from Article.
N_5.summary: Decides source_id stays inline on Article (no dedicated /articles/{id}/source route); flags that whether Source is itself a top-level resource is still open.

N_6.question: Right, I agree that we shouldn't assume Source is a resource just because Article references it. Let's look at Source next. In this application, users might want to browse or filter articles by source, but I'm not sure whether that alone is enough to make it a top-level resource. What would you consider when deciding whether Source deserves its own /sources endpoint?
N_6.answer: A few things I'd weigh: does Source have its own attributes worth fetching independently — name, URL, credibility rating, logo — things a client might want without going through an article at all? Does anything besides Article reference it, or will it always be reached via an article? And do clients need to browse sources themselves (a directory of sources), versus just filtering articles by one? Filtering alone doesn't require a /sources endpoint — a source_id query param on /articles covers that. It's the standalone-browsing and standalone-attribute needs that would justify it [N_5].
N_6.summary: Lays out criteria (standalone attributes, cross-resource references, standalone browsing) for deciding whether Source should be a top-level resource.

N_7.question: That distinction helps. I think Source probably does deserve to be a top-level resource in my case. A source would have its own metadata like name, URL, and possibly other information, and I can see the frontend eventually having a source directory or source-specific page. So would you model it simply as /sources alongside /articles, with /articles?source_id=... for filtering, rather than nesting articles under sources?
N_7.answer: Agreed — /sources alongside /articles is the right shape, especially once Source has its own directory/detail page [N_6]. Nesting (/sources/{id}/articles) would only make sense if articles were unreachable without a source context, but Article already stands alone. Filtering stays as /articles?source_id=..., the same source_id we already settled on [N_5] — just now backed by a real /sources resource instead of an opaque foreign key.
N_7.summary: Decides Source is a top-level resource: /sources alongside /articles, with /articles?source_id=... for filtering, not nested under sources.

N_8.question: Okay, that gives us a consistent pattern for Article and Source. Let's move to Topic. Since topics are curated and independently useful for filtering and browsing, I'm leaning toward making Topic a top-level resource too. Would you agree, and how would you structure the relationship with articles?
N_8.answer: Agreed — same pattern applies: /topics alongside /articles and /sources, giving Topic its own detail/browse page. The Article relationship stays exactly as we already decided [N_4] — POST/DELETE /articles/{id}/topics/{topic_id} for assignment, /articles?topic_id=... for filtering — nothing changes there, it's just now backed by a real /topics resource with its own metadata instead of an opaque tag.
N_8.summary: Decides Topic is a top-level resource (/topics), with the Article relationship unchanged from the N_4 dedicated-endpoint decision.

N_9.question: That seems consistent. So at this point we have three independent resources: Article, Source, and Topic, with relationships between them handled explicitly. Let's look at Entity next. Since entities are extracted by the NLP pipeline rather than curated by users, I'm thinking they might be quite different from Topic. Should Entity still be a top-level resource, or would you keep it primarily accessible through articles?
N_9.answer: Keep it as-is — Entity stays the read-only sub-resource under Article, not top-level [N_3], because it's derived data, not something users curate the way Topic is. That said, you'll probably still want a read-only filter like /articles?entity=... for 'show me articles mentioning X,' without giving Entity its own top-level collection or independent lifecycle. So the real distinction isn't 'sub-resource vs. top-level,' it's 'no independent write operations' — reads can still happen from more than one angle.
N_9.summary: Reaffirms Entity stays a read-only sub-resource under Article, distinguishing no-write-access from top-level-vs-not.

N_10.question: I agree with keeping Entity read-only, but I'm not completely convinced that means it shouldn't be top-level. Since we want to link entities to Wikidata and may eventually have entity-specific metadata, an entity could have attributes that are useful independently of a particular article. Would it be better to make Entity a read-only top-level resource, while still preventing clients from creating or modifying entities? That would also give us a clean /entities/{id} for entity details and Wikidata information.
N_10.answer: Good push — that reasoning changes it. If entities need canonical identity for Wikidata linking and their own metadata, they need one addressable record, not duplicated per-article mentions. I'd revise the earlier call [N_3]: make Entity a genuine top-level resource with GET /entities/{id} and /entities, but keep it read-only for clients — the NLP pipeline stays the only writer. /articles/{id}/entities stays too, as a convenience view scoped to one article, backed by the same canonical records.
N_10.summary: Revises the N_3 decision: Entity becomes a read-only top-level resource for canonical identity/Wikidata linking, not just an Article sub-resource.

N_11.question: That sounds like a better model. So Entity has its own lifecycle from the API's perspective, even though its lifecycle is controlled by the NLP pipeline rather than by clients. I think that also raises a question about the article-entity relationship. Since an entity can appear in many articles, should we represent that relationship as a simple many-to-many link, or do we need a separate ArticleEntity relationship with metadata such as confidence, mention count, or the position of the entity in the article?
N_11.answer: Yes — confidence, mention count, and position are facts about the relationship itself, not about either Article or Entity alone, so you need an association object rather than a plain join table [N_3]. Call it something like ArticleEntity (or 'mentions'): still populated only by the NLP pipeline, still read-only to clients, but its own row per (article, entity) pair. Practically it can stay embedded in the existing /articles/{id}/entities response — you don't need a fourth top-level resource for it, just richer objects in that collection instead of bare entity references [N_10].
N_11.summary: Decides the Article-Entity relationship needs an association object (ArticleEntity) for confidence/mention_count/position, embedded in /articles/{id}/entities.

N_12.question: That makes sense. I like keeping ArticleEntity as an internal association rather than exposing another top-level resource. For the API representation, would you return the full entity object inside /articles/{id}/entities, or something smaller like the entity ID plus the relationship metadata? I'm thinking about response size if an article contains a lot of entities.
N_12.answer: Return ID plus the relationship metadata, not the full entity object — something like {entity_id, name, type, confidence, mention_count, position}. Name and type are cheap and useful for display without a second round-trip; everything else (Wikidata links, full attributes) belongs behind GET /entities/{id} now that it's addressable [N_10]. That keeps /articles/{id}/entities bounded even for entity-dense articles, and avoids duplicating entity data that could drift out of sync across every article that mentions it.
N_12.summary: Decides /articles/{id}/entities returns entity ID plus display fields and relationship metadata, not the full entity object.
N_12.reference: Slim entity representation in article response

N_13.question: I think we should decide how the main article representation should look now. Would you keep relationships like source_id and topic_ids as simple IDs in the article response, or would you include some embedded information about those related resources as well?
N_13.answer: Keep source_id and topic_ids as plain IDs by default [N_12] — same reasoning as the entity call. Embedding full objects would duplicate data that's already addressable via /sources/{id} and /topics/{id}, and blow up response size for articles tagged with many topics. If the frontend wants to avoid extra round-trips, add an optional ?include=source,topics expansion param rather than embedding by default.
N_13.summary: Decides Article representation keeps source_id/topic_ids as plain IDs by default, with an optional ?include= expansion param.
N_13.reference: Plain IDs by default, optional include param

N_14.question: I like the include approach. It gives us a predictable default representation while still letting the frontend request richer responses when it actually needs them. One concern: if we support ?include=source,topics, should we also support nested includes, or should we deliberately keep it to one level? For example, I wouldn't want something like include=source.articles.topics to accidentally produce a huge response.
N_14.answer: Good instinct — one level only, no dot-paths like source.articles.topics. That's exactly the kind of unbounded expansion we've been trying to avoid with response size, and it's worse than just large: that particular chain could even cycle back (an article's source's other articles' topics...), so it's structurally dangerous to allow, not just wasteful. I'd validate include against a fixed allow-list of top-level relation names — source, topics, maybe entities later — and reject requests with dotted or unrecognized values with a 400, rather than silently ignoring them, so clients get clear feedback instead of confusing partial responses.
N_14.summary: Decides ?include= is limited to one level, validated against an allow-list, with unsupported values rejected via 400 rather than silently ignored.
N_14.reference: Include param limited to one level, rejects invalid

N_15.question: Yes, I agree. I'd prefer rejecting unsupported includes rather than silently ignoring them, since silently ignoring a client request could make debugging confusing. That also makes me think about pagination. For /articles, /sources, /topics, and /entities, should we use the same pagination approach and response format across all collections?
N_15.answer: Yes — same pagination shape and response envelope everywhere, no exceptions per resource. I'd go cursor-based rather than offset/limit, since Article in particular will keep growing and offset pagination drifts (skips or repeats items) under concurrent inserts — cursor-based avoids that, and using it uniformly means the frontend doesn't need different pagination logic per collection. Something like {data: [...], pagination: {next_cursor, has_more}} as the shared envelope across /articles [N_3], /sources [N_7], /topics [N_8], and /entities [N_10].
N_15.summary: Decides on a consistent cursor-based pagination approach and response envelope across all four collection endpoints.

N_16.question: I agree with using cursor pagination consistently. One thing I want to clarify before we settle it: what should the cursor actually encode? For example, should it be based on a stable field like (created_at, id), or would you use something else? I want to make sure pagination remains deterministic when multiple records have the same timestamp.
N_16.answer: Yes — (created_at, id) as a composite [N_15], with id purely as a deterministic tiebreaker for equal timestamps, not because ordering by ID itself matters. Encode both values into an opaque cursor (e.g. base64 of {created_at, id}) rather than exposing them as separate raw query params — that keeps the internal representation free to change later and stops clients from hand-crafting cursors. The query becomes WHERE (created_at, id) > (:cursor_created_at, :cursor_id) ORDER BY created_at, id, which stays correct and index-friendly with a compound index on those two columns.
N_16.summary: Decides the pagination cursor encodes an opaque (created_at, id) composite, with id as a deterministic tiebreaker.

N_17.question: That makes sense. I'd also like to think about whether created_at is actually the right ordering field for every resource. For articles it seems natural, but for something like Topic or Entity, records might be updated or merged later. Would you still use (created_at, id) uniformly for all collections, or should the pagination strategy allow a resource-specific ordering field?
N_17.answer: Keep the mechanism uniform — same opaque cursor, same (field, id) composite pattern [N_16] — but let the actual ordering field vary by resource. Article's natural default is created_at, but Topic and Entity might default to updated_at instead, since a merge or curation edit is what actually makes a record 'recent' for those. One thing worth raising as its own question rather than solving now: if Entity records get merged, does the old ID redirect, tombstone, or just disappear? That affects both cursor stability and any client that's already cached a stale entity ID.
N_17.summary: Decides the cursor mechanism stays uniform but the ordering field is resource-specific; raises entity-merge ID stability as a separate open question.
N_17.reference: Resource-specific ordering field; entity-merge question raised

N_18.question: That's a good point about entity merging. I think we should keep that as an open design question rather than mix it into pagination right now. For the pagination mechanism itself, though, I think we should define the API contract clearly: the cursor should encode the ordering value and ID, while each resource can choose its default ordering field. Before we move on, would you recommend allowing clients to choose the ordering field with something like ?sort=updated_at, or should we expose only a small allow-list of predefined sort options per resource?
N_18.answer: Small allow-list per resource, not free-form. Client-supplied field names risk expensive unindexed sorts, and break the guaranteed id tiebreaker if clients could omit it — same kind of unbounded-surface problem as the include param [N_14]. Something like sort=created_at|-created_at for Article and sort=updated_at|-updated_at for Topic/Entity, validated against an enum, with id silently appended as the tiebreaker regardless of what the client picks.
N_18.summary: Decides sort options are exposed as a small per-resource allow-list, not free-form client-chosen fields, with id always appended as tiebreaker.

N_19.question: That seems reasonable. I like keeping the sorting surface explicit so we can guarantee the required indexes and deterministic pagination. Let's move on from pagination for now. We haven't really discussed authentication yet. Since this API will eventually have user-specific features like personalized articles, saved content, and the research chatbot, how would you approach authentication and authorization at the API level?
N_19.answer: I'd split it into two layers: authentication (proving who's calling) and authorization (what they're allowed to do). For authentication, use token-based auth via a proper provider — OAuth2/OIDC or a managed auth service — rather than rolling your own session/password handling; a bearer JWT is the common default. For authorization, given what you've described sounds user-scoped rather than role-heavy, simple ownership checks (a user can only touch their own data) probably beat a full RBAC system for now. Keep this orthogonal to what we've already designed [N_1]: Article/Source/Topic/Entity stay public-readable, while user-scoped resources like saved content or chat history live under something like /me/..., with the auth layer enforcing that the token's subject matches.
N_19.summary: Opens the authentication/authorization design thread: token-based auth, ownership-based authorization, kept orthogonal to the existing public resource model.

N_20.question: I agree with separating authentication from authorization. For the first version, I also don't think we need complex RBAC if most of the private data is user-owned. One thing I'm unsure about is the public/private boundary. If Article, Source, Topic, and Entity are publicly readable, should we make those endpoints completely unauthenticated, or would you still authenticate requests when a user is logged in so we can support things like personalization, rate limiting, or usage tracking?
N_20.answer: Still accept an optional token on those public endpoints — validate it if present, but don't require it. That lets you attach user context for personalization and per-user rate limits when someone's logged in [N_19], while anonymous requests fall back to IP-based limits. One thing worth watching: if personalization changes the response body (e.g. an is_saved flag on articles), you can't cache that response the same way for everyone anymore — caching needs to vary by auth state or bypass cache entirely for authenticated requests, or you risk leaking one user's personalization into another user's cached response.
N_20.summary: Decides public endpoints accept an optional bearer token for personalization/rate limiting, and flags a caching risk when personalization varies the response body.
N_20.reference: Optional auth on public endpoints; caching risk flagged

N_21.question: That's a good point about caching personalized responses. I'd probably keep the default public representation identical for authenticated and anonymous users, and expose personalization explicitly when needed rather than changing /articles implicitly based on the token. For example, would you prefer something like /me/articles/saved for saved articles, instead of adding is_saved to every public article response? That seems like it would keep caching and resource semantics cleaner.
N_21.answer: Yes — /me/articles/saved as an explicit endpoint is cleaner. Keeping /articles identical for every caller means it's fully cacheable (e.g. by a CDN) with zero auth-based variation, and personalization becomes its own explicit, separately-cached endpoint instead of a hidden variant of a public one. This also plays nicely with the earlier optional-token call [N_20] — you can still validate a token on /articles purely for rate-limiting purposes without letting it touch the response body at all, keeping those two concerns fully decoupled.
N_21.summary: Revises the optional-token decision: personalization is exposed via explicit endpoints like /me/articles/saved rather than varying public responses by auth state.
N_21.reference: Personalization via explicit /me endpoints, not implicit response variation

N_22.question: That separation is clear. I think we should define the /me boundary more carefully before implementing it. If we have saved articles and chat history under /me, would you make /me a general user-scoped namespace for all private resources, or would you still expose /users/{user_id} for cases where one authenticated user needs to access another user's public profile or data?
N_22.answer: Treat /me purely as a convenience alias for 'the authenticated caller,' not a separate resource type — internally it resolves to /users/{token_subject}. Keep /users/{user_id} as the general resource for public profile data (name, avatar, public activity), accessible to anyone. But private sub-resources like saved articles and chat history should live only under /me/... [N_21] and not be exposed under /users/{id}/... for other users at all — there's no described use case for one user seeing another's saved articles, so don't build that permission surface until you actually need it.
N_22.summary: Decides /me is a convenience alias for /users/{token_subject}; /users/{user_id} is the general public-profile resource; private data stays exclusive to /me.
N_22.reference: /me as alias, /users/{id} as general public profile

N_23.question: That seems like a good boundary. So /users/{user_id} represents the public user resource, while /me/... is just an authenticated-user convenience for private operations. One thing I want to clarify: if /me internally resolves to /users/{token_subject}, should clients ever be allowed to modify their own public profile through /me — for example PATCH /me — or should profile updates always use /users/{user_id}?
N_23.answer: Keep it symmetric with the alias framing [N_22] — allow PATCH /me too, but implement it as a thin passthrough to the exact same handler as PATCH /users/{token_subject}, not a separate code path. That way /me isn't special-cased to reads only, and the underlying rule stays simple: writing to /users/{id} is permitted only when id matches the token's subject, whether the client reached it via /me or the explicit ID.
N_23.summary: Decides PATCH /me is a passthrough alias to PATCH /users/{token_subject} using the identical handler; writes gated by token-subject match.

N_24.question: That keeps the semantics consistent. I like the idea of having /me resolve to the same underlying resource and handler rather than creating separate behavior. For PATCH /users/{id}, though, should we allow clients to update only a fixed set of profile fields, or would you use a generic partial-update mechanism and validate the fields dynamically?
N_24.answer: Fixed, explicit whitelist [N_23] — validate against a small set of user-editable fields (e.g. display_name, bio, avatar_url) at the schema level, not a generic dynamic mechanism that accepts arbitrary field names. A generic approach risks mass assignment — a client slipping role or verified into the payload and having it silently applied. And consistent with how we handled unsupported include values [N_14]: reject requests containing unknown fields rather than silently dropping them, so clients get clear feedback instead of assuming a field was applied when it wasn't.
N_24.summary: Decides PATCH /users/{id} validates against a fixed field whitelist to prevent mass assignment, rejecting unknown fields with 400.
N_24.reference: Fixed whitelist for profile PATCH, reject unknown fields

N_25.question: I agree. I think we should apply the same principle to the other write operations too. For example, when we add saved articles or topic assignments, should the API reject duplicate POSTs and missing DELETEs, or should those operations be idempotent so repeated requests simply leave the desired state unchanged?
N_25.answer: That's a related but distinct principle from the whitelist call [N_24] — that one was about which fields can be written, this is about how retries behave — but same instinct applies: predictable, well-specified contracts. I'd make these idempotent, not duplicate-rejecting: POST /me/articles/saved/{article_id} should succeed whether or not it was already saved, and DELETE should return 204 whether or not it existed — no 409 for 'already saved,' no 404 for 'already removed.' That's actually what we implicitly assumed for topic assignment already [N_4]; this just makes it explicit and applies it consistently everywhere, including ArticleEntity. Reserve real conflict errors for genuine object-creation endpoints, where a duplicate really would be a distinct resource.
N_25.summary: Decides relationship-toggle write operations (saved articles, topic assignments) are idempotent, formalizing what was already implicit for topic assignment.

N_26.question: I agree with making those state-changing relationship operations idempotent. That should make retries much safer, especially if the client loses the response and repeats the request. For POST /me/articles/saved/{article_id}, though, I'm wondering about the choice of POST. Since the operation is essentially "make this relationship exist" and is idempotent, would PUT /me/articles/saved/{article_id} be more semantically appropriate? Or is there a reason you'd still prefer POST here?
N_26.answer: Yes, PUT is more semantically correct here — PUT means 'set the resource at this URI to this state,' which is exactly 'this relationship should exist,' and it's defined as idempotent by the HTTP spec itself, matching what we already decided [N_25]. POST is really for appending to a collection or non-idempotent actions without a natural target URI — neither applies since /me/articles/saved/{article_id} already names the exact resource. Worth going back and applying the same fix to topic assignment too [N_4] — PUT/DELETE /articles/{id}/topics/{topic_id}, not POST/DELETE, for the same reason. This generalizes into a standing rule: any endpoint representing 'this specific relationship should exist' uses PUT, not POST.
N_26.summary: Decides PUT (not POST) is the correct verb for idempotent relationship-existence endpoints; revises both the topic-assignment and saved-article verb choices.

N_27.question: Yes, let's make that a general relationship rule: PUT creates/ensures a specific relationship exists, and DELETE removes it, with both being idempotent. That also makes me think about the distinction between relationships and actions. For example, saving an article fits naturally as a relationship, but something like triggering article summarization or asking the research chatbot doesn't really represent a resource relationship. Would you recommend modeling those as action endpoints, such as POST /articles/{id}/summarize, or is there a better REST pattern for operations that trigger processing?
N_27.answer: I'd avoid a literal verb-shaped URI like /articles/{id}/summarize where possible — model the output as a resource instead: POST /articles/{id}/summaries creates a new Summary, a genuinely distinct resource each time, so ordinary POST-for-creation semantics apply, not the idempotent PUT pattern we just settled [N_26]. If it's slow, return 202 Accepted with a resource you can poll rather than blocking. Same idea for the chatbot [N_2]: POST /conversations creates a session, POST /conversations/{id}/messages appends to it — actions become resource creation under the hood, even when they read like verbs from the client's side.
N_27.summary: Decides processing-triggering operations (summarization, chatbot) are modeled as resource creation, not verb-shaped action URIs.

N_28.question: For summaries, though, I'm not sure whether we actually want multiple Summary resources for the same article. We might eventually regenerate a summary with a different model or prompt, but the application probably only needs one current summary most of the time. Would you still create a new Summary for every generation, or would you model the summary as a sub-resource that can be replaced with PUT?
N_28.answer: I'd keep Summary as a real collection — POST creates a new one each generation [N_27] — since you mentioned wanting to regenerate with different models or prompts, which implies wanting to keep and possibly compare past versions eventually, even if the UI only shows one right now. On top of that, add a lightweight GET /articles/{id}/summary (singular) that just returns whichever generation is current — a convenience read, not a separate write-target. That way the client that only cares about 'the' summary never needs to know about the underlying history, but you're not throwing away data you'll likely want later.
N_28.summary: Decides Summary stays a collection preserving generation history, with a convenience singular GET endpoint for the current summary.

N_29.question: I'd like to clarify what makes a summary 'current.' If a new generation is created, does it automatically become current, or should there be an explicit operation to promote a particular summary version? This could matter if we later generate summaries asynchronously or with different models.
N_29.answer: Make it explicit, not automatic — a new generation creates a Summary but doesn't become current until a separate operation promotes it, reusing the same PUT pattern we already settled [N_26]: something like PUT /articles/{id}/summary/current with a body naming the summary_id to promote. This avoids a real race: if generations run async and out of order [N_27], 'most recently created' isn't necessarily 'most recently finished' or 'best,' so auto-promoting on creation could surface a stale or lower-quality result. It's also consistent with a pattern that's run through most of this conversation — explicit over implicit, whether that's include params, sort allow-lists, field whitelists, or now this.
N_29.summary: Decides summary promotion to current is explicit (PUT naming summary_id), never automatic, avoiding async out-of-order promotion races.

N_30.question: Since summaries are generated by the system but the current summary affects what users see, would you make PUT /articles/{id}/summary/current an internal/admin operation, or should an authenticated user be able to choose the current summary?
N_30.answer: Admin/editorial operation, not something any authenticated user can trigger — this is different from the ownership-based cases we've built so far [N_19], because promoting a summary changes what every visitor sees on a public resource, not something scoped to the caller's own data. I'd gate PUT /articles/{id}/summary/current behind a minimal role check (e.g. an is_editor flag), rather than 'any logged-in user.' That's a narrow exception, though, not a reason to build out full RBAC — most of the API still only needs the ownership check we already settled on.
N_30.summary: Decides summary promotion requires an elevated editorial role, not any authenticated user, as a narrow exception to the ownership-based authorization default.
N_30.reference: Editorial role required for summary promotion

N_31.question: I'm also wondering about the summary generation itself. If the API accepts a request to generate a summary and processing is asynchronous, should POST /articles/{id}/summaries immediately create a Summary with something like status: pending, or would you model the generation as a separate job resource and create the Summary only after processing succeeds?
N_31.answer: Separate Job resource, not a pending Summary — POST /articles/{id}/summary-jobs creates a job (status: pending/processing/completed/failed), and only on success does it produce an actual Summary, referenced from the completed job. That keeps Summary meaning strictly 'a finished, usable artifact,' never an empty placeholder, and mirrors the clean separation we just drew between generation and promotion [N_29]. It also gives a natural polling target — GET /articles/{id}/summary-jobs/{job_id} — without the Summary collection accumulating pending or failed entries [N_27].
N_31.summary: Decides async summary generation uses a separate Job resource; Summary is only created upon job success.
N_31.reference: Job resource separate from Summary artifact

N_32.question: If we later have other asynchronous operations - entity extraction, article ingestion, embedding generation, etc. - would you make Job a generic top-level resource like /jobs/{id}, or keep jobs nested under the resource that created them, as with /articles/{id}/summary-jobs/{job_id}?
N_32.answer: Generic top-level resource — /jobs/{id}, with a job_type field (summary_generation, entity_extraction, ingestion, embedding, etc.) and a reference to whatever it produced. That avoids re-implementing status tracking, polling, and lifecycle handling separately for every future async operation type [N_31]. You can still offer a convenience filtered view like GET /articles/{id}/jobs for 'jobs related to this article' — the same pattern we used for Entity: a canonical top-level resource with a scoped nested view, not two separate resource types [N_10].
N_32.summary: Decides Job becomes a generic top-level resource covering all async operation types, mirroring the Entity canonical+nested-view pattern.

N_33.question: Since different job types can produce completely different resources, would you use a generic result_id/result_type pair, or would you model the output relationship differently?
N_33.answer: result_type + result_id, yes — that's the natural fit for a genuinely polymorphic reference, since Job can point to a Summary, an entity-extraction result, an embedding, or whatever comes later [N_32]. I'd also include a ready-to-use link alongside those two raw fields — something like result: {type: "summary", id: "...", url: "/articles/{article_id}/summaries/{id}"} — so clients don't have to hand-construct the URL themselves from type + id, same self-descriptive spirit as the job resource itself.
N_33.summary: Decides Job output uses a polymorphic result_type/result_id pair plus a ready-to-use result URL.

N_34.question: For failed jobs, though, there won't be a result_id. Would you keep the same result field as null, and put failure details in something like an error object? Also, should those error details be safe for clients to expose directly, or should we separate internal error information from the public job response?
N_34.answer: Yes — result: null plus an error object on failure [N_33]. And yes, definitely separate the two: never return raw exception messages, stack traces, or internal service details in the public job response — that's an information-leakage risk and unhelpful to clients anyway. Return a small curated shape instead, like error: {code: 'MODEL_TIMEOUT', message: 'Summary generation timed out, please try again.'}, using a fixed error-code taxonomy [N_24], similar in spirit to the field whitelist we used for profile updates. Log the full internal detail server-side, correlated by job ID, for your own debugging — clients never see it.
N_34.summary: Decides failed jobs use result:null plus a curated client-safe error object; internal error details stay server-side only.
N_34.reference: Curated error object, internal details logged only

N_35.question: That makes sense. The job response can remain a stable public contract while the server logs retain the diagnostic details. I think we have enough of the resource model now to start thinking about the actual API structure. Before we implement anything, would you recommend writing the API contract first - for example with OpenAPI - and then implementing the endpoints from that contract, or should we implement the core resources first and document them as we go?
N_35.answer: Contract-first, definitely — write the OpenAPI spec before implementing, especially given how many things we revised along the way today: Entity's resource status [N_10], the assignment verb choice [N_26], Job's shape [N_32]. Catching those kinds of inconsistencies in a spec is cheap; catching them after code and clients depend on the wrong shape is expensive. It also gives you one artifact both frontend and backend can build against in parallel, and you can generate mock servers or client SDKs straight from it. I'd treat today's decisions as the input to that spec — the next concrete step is turning this conversation into an actual OpenAPI document.
N_35.summary: Decides to write the OpenAPI contract before implementation; marks the resource-modeling goal as achieved.

N_36.question: Before we write the OpenAPI spec, I think we should review the decisions we've made and check for inconsistencies or missing pieces. Could we first make a concise list of the resources, endpoints, and main rules we've settled on, and then use that as the basis for the spec?
N_36.answer: Done — I've put together a full resource/endpoint/rules review in a file. Short version: we've settled Article, Source, Topic, and Entity as resources with their endpoints and ten cross-cutting rules, but the review surfaced three real gaps — User was never formally decided as top-level, Conversation is just two named endpoints with no design behind them, and Source's pagination ordering field was assumed rather than decided.
N_36.summary: Produces a consolidated review of resources, endpoints, and rules, surfacing three unresolved gaps (User, Conversation, Source ordering field).

N_37.question: Starting with User: given that users have their own public profile data and we already have /users/{user_id} plus /me, would you formally consider User a top-level resource?
N_37.answer: Yes — formally, User is top-level. We've been treating it that way in practice since N_19 anyway: GET /users/{user_id} for public profile data, PATCH restricted to the owner or via the /me alias [N_23], validated against the whitelist we already settled [N_24]. This closes out the last open item from the original resource list [N_2].
N_37.summary: Formally confirms User as a top-level resource, resolving the last open candidate from the original resource list.

N_38.question: How would you model a conversation and its messages? In particular, what would you put in the Conversation and Message resources, and how would you handle ownership and message history?
N_38.answer: Keep it minimal: Conversation needs just id, owner (implicit via token, not a client-settable field), created_at, and maybe a nullable title for v1. Message needs id, conversation_id, role (user/assistant), content, and created_at — a simple linear history, no threading needed yet. On ownership: given the private-resource rule we already settled [N_22], these should actually live under /me/conversations and /me/conversations/{id}/messages, not top-level /conversations as I sketched back at [N_27] — that was an oversight on my part, worth fixing now that we're doing the review pass. Message creation stays plain POST (each message is a genuinely new, distinct item, not a relationship-toggle), and message history is just cursor-paginated [N_15] in creation order.
N_38.summary: Models Conversation and Message minimally for v1, moves them under /me/, and revises the N_27 top-level /conversations naming.

N_39.question: A user message will eventually trigger an assistant response asynchronously. Should POST /me/conversations/{id}/messages create only the user message and return immediately, with a separate job handling the assistant response, or should the endpoint itself represent the whole exchange?
N_39.answer: Just the user message, returned immediately — then a separate Job handles generating the assistant's response [N_31], the same pattern as summary generation. The Job's result, once complete, is itself a new Message (role: assistant) POSTed into the same conversation, not something bolted onto the original request/response. That keeps message creation uniform — every message is just a POST, whether it came from the client or the pipeline [N_38] — and avoids one endpoint trying to represent two different things happening at two different times.
N_39.summary: Decides message creation and assistant-response generation are split: POST creates only the user message, a separate Job produces the assistant Message.
N_39.reference: User message immediate, assistant response via Job

N_40.question: For the Job itself, should we expose a generic job endpoint for the chatbot response just like we do for summaries, or should the conversation response include a direct link to the job so the client doesn't have to discover it separately?
N_40.answer: Both — keep /jobs/{id} as the canonical endpoint [N_32], but have the POST /me/conversations/{id}/messages response embed a direct link to the job it triggered, not just the created message. Something like {message: {...}, job: {id, url: "/jobs/{id}"}} — mirrors the same self-descriptive link pattern we used for the job's own result field [N_33], just applied at the trigger point instead of the completion point. That way the client never has to guess or separately list jobs to find the one tied to this exchange.
N_40.summary: Decides message-creation responses embed a direct link to the triggered Job, in addition to the canonical /jobs/{id} endpoint.
N_40.reference: Job link embedded in message response

N_41.question: If the assistant-generation job fails, the user message already exists but there won't be an assistant message. Should the conversation simply remain in that state with the failed job being the source of truth, or should the system create an assistant message indicating that generation failed?
N_41.answer: I'd create a synthetic assistant Message on failure too — role: assistant, a friendly fallback like 'Sorry, I couldn't generate a response, please try again,' plus an explicit flag like status: 'failed' referencing the Job. If you rely on clients discovering the failed job separately [N_40], every client has to duplicate the same error-detection logic instead of just rendering the message history it already knows how to render. This keeps failure representation explicit rather than an implicit gap the client has to reconcile [N_34] — just make sure the failure flag is unambiguous so a client can't mistake it for a real generated response.
N_41.summary: Decides job failures produce a synthetic assistant Message with an explicit failed status, rather than a silent gap in the conversation.

N_42.question: Would you add a more explicit message status such as status: 'completed' | 'failed' to every message, with the failed message also carrying the job_id? Or would you keep status only on failed messages?
N_42.answer: Every message, not just failed ones — status: 'completed' | 'failed', present uniformly, the same way Job's result field stays present (as null) rather than disappearing on failure [N_34]. An optional field that only shows up sometimes is a worse contract than one that's always there with a predictable value — clients would rather check a value than check for a field's existence. job_id would be present (possibly null) on assistant messages specifically, tracing back to whichever Job produced or attempted to produce that message.
N_42.summary: Decides status is present uniformly on every message, not just failures, plus a nullable job_id on assistant messages.
N_42.reference: Uniform status field on every message

N_43.question: My instinct is that POST /me/conversations/{id}/messages should only accept role: user, while assistant messages can only be created internally by the chatbot pipeline. Would you enforce that at the API boundary?
N_43.answer: Yes, absolutely — enforce it server-side, not just as a convention. Simplest approach: don't even accept a role field on that endpoint; every message POSTed there is hardcoded role: 'user' internally, and assistant messages are only ever created by the pipeline's own internal write path, never through the public API. Same mass-assignment concern as the profile whitelist [N_24] — if a client could set role: 'assistant' directly, they could forge fake model output inside their own conversation history.
N_43.summary: Decides the public message endpoint hardcodes role:user server-side; assistant messages can only be created via the internal pipeline.

N_44.question: Should users be allowed to delete or edit their messages, or should conversation messages be immutable once created?
N_44.answer: Immutable, no PATCH/DELETE on individual messages — the assistant's response was generated from the exact prior content, so editing it after the fact would silently desync what was asked from what was answered. If a user wants to change something, they send a new message rather than rewriting history — simpler than reconciliation logic, and it mirrors exactly what we already decided for Summary regeneration [N_28]: don't mutate in place, create a new record. I would allow deleting the whole Conversation (removing the entire thread), just not individual messages within one — that avoids leaving a conversation with confusing gaps.
N_44.summary: Decides messages are immutable once created; conversation-level deletion is allowed but not per-message edit/delete.

N_45.question: When a conversation is deleted, should that be a hard delete of the conversation and all its messages, or would you prefer a soft-delete approach so the data can be recovered or retained for audit purposes?
N_45.answer: Soft-delete, at least for v1 — a deleted_at timestamp that excludes the conversation from normal listing and access, but keeps the underlying data intact. That's actually in tension with what we just praised about immutability [N_44] — a hard delete would destroy exactly the audit trail we said was valuable — so soft-delete keeps that benefit while still satisfying the user's expectation that 'delete' makes it disappear. I'd leave the actual retention/purge policy (how long deleted data is kept, and whether there's a separate hard-delete path for privacy/legal requests) as an open question rather than deciding it now — that's a real compliance question, not just an API shape one, and deserves its own dedicated discussion.
N_45.summary: Decides Conversation deletion is soft-delete for v1, preserving the audit-trail benefit of immutable messages; retention policy left open.
N_45.reference: Soft-delete for Conversation, retention policy open

N_46.question: For Source, would you use created_at as the default ordering, or updated_at?
N_46.answer: created_at, as the default — same reasoning as Article: Sources are added occasionally, and 'recently added source' is what most callers would expect from a default view of the collection. Unlike Topic and Entity, Source doesn't undergo merges or heavy ongoing curation [N_17], so created_at won't go stale as a default the way it would there. I'd still keep updated_at available through the sort allow-list [N_18] for anyone specifically wanting recently-edited sources, just not as the default.
N_46.summary: Decides Source's default pagination ordering field is created_at, with updated_at available as an allow-listed alternative.

N_47.question: What should happen when the NLP pipeline determines that two entities are actually the same entity? Would you keep the old entity as a redirect to the canonical one, or use a different approach?
N_47.answer: Redirect, not delete — mark the old Entity with status: 'merged' and a canonical_id pointing to the surviving record, the same pattern Wikidata itself uses [N_10]. GET /entities/{old_id} returns a redirect (e.g. a Location header or an explicit {status: 'merged', canonical_id} body) rather than 404 or stale data, so any existing links or citations still resolve. This also directly answers the concern that raised this question in the first place [N_17]: since the merged row isn't deleted, just flagged, cursor-based pagination stays stable — no gaps, no renumbering. ArticleEntity records referencing the old entity_id can resolve through the redirect at read-time rather than needing an immediate rewrite.
N_47.summary: Decides entity merges use a redirect pattern (status:merged + canonical_id), resolving the entity-merge open question raised at N_17.

N_48.question: For a merged entity, should GET /entities include the old status: 'merged' records, or should the collection return only active canonical entities by default?
N_48.answer: Active/canonical only by default — a caller listing GET /entities almost always wants the current set, not old aliases sitting next to their canonical replacements. I'd add an explicit opt-in like ?status=all or ?include_merged=true for the cases that actually need to see merged records (admin tooling, data reconciliation), rather than showing everything by default. This doesn't conflict with keeping merged rows around for cursor stability [N_47] — that's about not deleting or renumbering rows, while the default filter is just a WHERE clause on the collection query; direct GET /entities/{merged_id} still resolves via redirect either way.
N_48.summary: Decides GET /entities excludes merged records by default, with an explicit opt-in to include them.
N_48.reference: Merged entities excluded from default collection view

N_49.question: Should we design the API as versioned from the beginning, for example /api/v1/articles, or keep the URLs unversioned and introduce versioning only when we actually need a breaking change?
N_49.answer: Version from day one — /api/v1/articles, even though it feels like premature ceremony with only one version so far. Retrofitting versioning after clients depend on unversioned URLs is far more disruptive than carrying the prefix from the start. Today's own session is a good argument for this: we revised Entity's top-level status [N_10], the relationship verb [N_26], and Job's shape [N_32] — multiple times, just during design. The odds of needing an actual breaking change once this ships are real, and you'll want a clean way to introduce v2 without breaking v1 clients. I'd keep it at the URL path level rather than header-based versioning — simpler for clients, caching, and debugging, even if it's less 'elegant.'
N_49.summary: Decides the API is versioned from the start via URL path (/api/v1/), citing multiple in-session revisions as evidence for future breaking changes.

N_50.question: We've mentioned {data: [...], pagination: ...} for collections and {code, message} for errors, but we haven't defined whether single-resource responses should also use a data envelope. Would you use a consistent {data: ...} envelope for both single resources and collections, or return the resource directly for single-resource endpoints?
N_50.answer: Yes — {data: ...} uniformly, even for single resources: GET /articles/{id} returns {data: {...}}, not the bare object. That buys consistent client parsing logic regardless of endpoint shape, and leaves room to add top-level metadata later (deprecation notices, links, warnings) without a breaking change — the same reasoning that led us to wrap Job's result in extra structure rather than returning it bare [N_33]. It's a small bit of ceremony on every single-resource response, but it's exactly the kind of upfront consistency cost that's cheap now and expensive to retrofit later, same argument as versioning [N_49].
N_50.summary: Decides on a consistent {data: ...} envelope for both single-resource and collection responses.
N_50.reference: Consistent data envelope for all responses

SN_1.label: Design the REST API's resource model before implementing endpoints

SN_2.label: Which of User/Article/Source/Topic/Entity should be independent API resources?

SN_3.label: Model Article as top-level; Source many-to-one, Topic/Entity many-to-many with Entity as read-only derived sub-resource

SN_4.label: Manage Topic assignment via dedicated relationship endpoint, not nested article PATCH

SN_5.label: Keep source_id inline on Article representation; no dedicated /articles/{id}/source endpoint

SN_6.label: Source is a top-level resource: /sources alongside /articles, with /articles?source_id=... for filtering, not nested

SN_7.label: Topic is a top-level resource: /topics alongside /articles and /sources; Article relationship unchanged from N_4 decision

SN_8.label: Represent the Article-Entity relationship as an association object (ArticleEntity) with confidence/mention_count/position; embedded in /articles/{id}/entities, not a new top-level resource

SN_9.label: Article API responses should stay bounded in size even for entity-dense articles

SN_10.label: Return entity ID + name/type + relationship metadata inline in /articles/{id}/entities; full entity detail via GET /entities/{id}

SN_11.label: Keep source_id/topic_ids as plain ID references in Article representation by default; support optional ?include= expansion for embedding

SN_12.label: Limit ?include= expansion to one level; validate against an allow-list of top-level relation names; reject (400) dotted/unsupported values rather than silently ignoring them

SN_13.label: Use a consistent cursor-based pagination approach and response envelope across all collection endpoints

SN_14.label: Cursor encodes an opaque (created_at, id) composite; id is purely a deterministic tiebreaker for equal timestamps

SN_15.label: Keep pagination cursor mechanism uniform, but allow the ordering field to be resource-specific (created_at for Article, updated_at for Topic/Entity)

SN_16.label: How should Entity merges be represented (redirect, tombstone, alias), given effects on cursor stability and cached client references?

SN_17.label: Sort/ordering options must be validated against a fixed per-resource allow-list; arbitrary client-specified fields are not permitted

SN_18.label: Expose ?sort= as a per-resource enum (Article: created_at/-created_at; Topic/Entity: updated_at/-updated_at); id always appended as tiebreaker

SN_19.label: Design authentication and authorization for the API, covering user-specific features (personalized articles, saved content, research chatbot)

SN_20.label: Cached responses must not leak per-user personalization across users; caching strategy must vary by auth state or bypass cache for authenticated requests

SN_21.label: Public read endpoints accept an optional bearer token — validated if present for personalization/per-user rate limiting, not required; anonymous requests fall back to IP-based rate limiting

SN_22.label: Personalization (e.g. saved articles) exposed via explicit dedicated endpoints like /me/articles/saved rather than injected into public resource responses; public representations stay identical regardless of auth state

SN_23.label: /me is a convenience alias for /users/{token_subject}, not a separate resource type; /users/{user_id} exposes general public profile data; private sub-resources (saved articles, chat history) live only under /me/... and are never exposed under /users/{id}/... for other users

SN_24.label: Allow PATCH /me as a passthrough alias to PATCH /users/{token_subject} using the identical handler; write access to /users/{id} permitted only when id matches the token subject, whether reached via /me or explicit ID

SN_25.label: PATCH /users/{id} must not be vulnerable to mass assignment; only an explicit whitelist of fields may be updated

SN_26.label: PATCH /users/{id} validates against a fixed whitelist (display_name, bio, avatar_url); unknown fields are rejected with 400

SN_27.label: Relationship-toggle write operations (saved articles, topic assignments, etc.) are idempotent: POST succeeds regardless of prior state, DELETE returns 204 regardless of prior existence; conflict errors reserved for genuine object-creation endpoints

SN_28.label: Use PUT (not POST) for idempotent relationship-existence endpoints (saved articles, topic assignments, etc.); PUT signals 'set this resource to this state,' matching the already-decided idempotent semantics

SN_29.label: Model processing-triggering operations as resource creation (POST /articles/{id}/summaries creates a Summary; POST /conversations creates a session, POST /conversations/{id}/messages appends) rather than verb-shaped action URIs; async operations return 202 Accepted with a pollable resource

SN_30.label: Keep Summary as a collection (POST creates a new one per generation, preserving history); add a convenience GET /articles/{id}/summary (singular) returning the current/most-recent generation, not a separate write target

SN_31.label: Promoting a Summary to 'current' is an explicit operation (PUT /articles/{id}/summary/current naming the summary_id), never automatic on generation, to avoid async out-of-order promotion

SN_32.label: API behavior should favor explicit, client-controlled operations over implicit/automatic state changes, especially where async timing or generation source could produce surprising results

SN_33.label: Summary promotion (PUT /articles/{id}/summary/current) requires an elevated role (e.g. editor/admin), not just any authenticated user, since it affects shared public-facing content; remains a narrow exception rather than justifying full RBAC

SN_34.label: Async summary generation creates a separate Job resource (POST /articles/{id}/summary-jobs, status pending/processing/completed/failed); Summary is only created upon job success and referenced from the completed job

SN_35.label: Job becomes a generic top-level resource (/jobs/{id}) with a job_type field and result reference, covering summary generation and future async operations (entity extraction, ingestion, embedding); resource-scoped convenience views (e.g. GET /articles/{id}/jobs) filter the same underlying collection rather than being separate resource types, mirroring the Entity canonical+nested-view pattern

SN_36.label: Job's output is referenced via a polymorphic result_type + result_id pair, plus a ready-to-use result URL, rather than type-specific foreign keys

SN_37.label: On job failure, result is null and an error object is included with a curated, client-safe shape (fixed error-code taxonomy + generic message), not raw internal exception details

SN_38.label: Internal error details (stack traces, exception messages, internal service info) must never be exposed in public API responses; log full detail server-side correlated by job ID instead

SN_39.label: Write the API contract (OpenAPI) first, before implementation; treat today's decisions as input to that spec

SN_40.label: Is User a top-level API resource? (SN_2 never formally closed on this point)

SN_41.label: User formally confirmed as a top-level resource (/users/{user_id}); already in practical use since N_19 for auth/profile design

SN_42.label: Model Conversation (id, owner via token, created_at, nullable title) and Message (id, conversation_id, role, content, created_at) simply for v1; Message creation is plain POST, not idempotent PUT, since it is not a relationship-toggle

SN_43.label: POST /me/conversations/{id}/messages creates only the user Message and returns immediately; a separate Job generates the assistant response, which becomes its own Message (role: assistant) once complete

SN_44.label: POST /me/conversations/{id}/messages response embeds a direct link to the triggered Job (job.id + job.url), rather than requiring the client to separately discover it; /jobs/{id} remains the canonical endpoint

SN_45.label: On assistant-generation job failure, create a synthetic assistant Message with a fallback content string and an explicit status:'failed' flag referencing the Job, rather than leaving a silent gap in the conversation

SN_46.label: Every Message carries status: 'completed'|'failed' uniformly (not only on failure), and assistant messages carry job_id (nullable) tracing back to the generating Job

SN_47.label: POST /me/conversations/{id}/messages must not allow clients to set role directly; assistant-authored messages may only be created via the internal pipeline write path, never through the public API

SN_48.label: The public message-creation endpoint hardcodes role:'user' server-side and ignores/rejects any client-supplied role field

SN_49.label: Messages are immutable once created (no PATCH/DELETE on individual messages); DELETE is only supported at the Conversation level (whole-thread deletion), consistent with the no-in-place-mutation pattern used for Summary regeneration

SN_50.label: Conversation deletion is soft-delete (deleted_at timestamp), excluded from listings but data retained, at least for v1

SN_51.label: What retention/purge policy applies to soft-deleted conversations, and is a separate hard-delete path needed for privacy/legal (e.g. GDPR erasure) requests?

SN_52.label: Source's default pagination ordering field is created_at (matching Article's reasoning); updated_at remains available via the sort allow-list but is not the default

SN_53.label: Entity merges use a redirect pattern: old Entity marked status:'merged' with canonical_id pointing to the surviving record; GET on the old ID returns redirect info rather than 404 or stale data; merged rows are not deleted, preserving cursor pagination stability

SN_54.label: GET /entities returns only active/canonical entities by default (excludes status:'merged'); an explicit opt-in (?status=all or ?include_merged=true) surfaces merged records for admin/reconciliation use cases; direct GET /entities/{id} on a merged ID still resolves via redirect regardless of the collection filter

SN_55.label: API is versioned from the start via URL path (/api/v1/...), not introduced later; URL-path versioning chosen over header-based versioning for simplicity

SN_56.label: Use a consistent {data: ...} envelope for both single-resource and collection responses, not a bare object for single resources; collections additionally carry pagination alongside data
